title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
This project set out to explore how quantum computing approaches the Max-Cut problem differently from classical methods. Using Google’s Cirq library, I implemented the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and compared it against brute force and greedy classical baselines across graphs ranging from 4 to 30 nodes.
My six measurable goals were: formulating Max-Cut as an Ising Hamiltonian, implementing QAOA in Cirq, simulating quantum circuits, building classical baselines, evaluating approximation ratios, and analyzing runtime scaling.

QAOA consistently outperformed greedy on smaller graphs but both methods degraded at larger sizes, an expected consequence of p=1 circuit depth.
The most striking result was runtime scaling. At n=30, brute force took 118 minutes while QAOA simulation took ~103 minutes. Projecting forward, brute force would take ~43 years at n=50. On real quantum hardware, that same QAOA circuit would run in microseconds.

title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
Reflection
The hardest part was finding research that explained expected results without giving away the implementation. Significant work constraints — four week-long field projects and a two-week remote dam maintenance assignment — made data collection difficult. The unexpected passing of my last close grandparent added further challenge during the project period.
The most surprising finding was QAOA occasionally losing to greedy. This turned out to be expected behavior at p=1 under classical simulation constraints and is not a flaw in the implementation.

title: QAOA Final Report: Quantum vs Classical Max-Cut
text:
What’s Next
Given more time I would run circuits on real quantum hardware via IBM Quantum, implement higher p values to show quality improvement with circuit depth, and benchmark against the Goemans-Williamson semidefinite programming approach.

title: QAOA Progress: Defining the Graph
text:
Last week I finally implement a virtual environment for my project and went about properly installing the libraries that I am into that environment. They are also frozen to the specific versions they were downloaded as so as to prevent any breaks do to updates later on. I also studies further into Google’s own cirq file regarding QAOA Maxcut and began running their implementation of this project to see what expected outputs should look like or would look like once my own implementation is complete. I’ve started with creating the graph and getting it to display properly, this has been a big frustration mainly due to initially using codespaces on github, giving up and cloning the repo onto my own hardware and that has been smoother sailing. My graph is on the left and the google graph is on the right. I have included line weights in my own graph as these will determine the number of cuts between each node. Google’s implementation leaves out the weighting of the edges.













Figure 1: Comparison of a randomly generated weighted graph and the Google Sycamore connectivity graph.

title: QAOA Progress: Cut Visualizations
text:
As part of the ongoing QAOA experiments, I have been generating cut visualizations across different graph sizes. For each graph, blue nodes are in partition 1 and red nodes are in partition 0. Green edges cross the partition boundary and contribute to the cut value. Gray edges connect nodes in the same partition and contribute nothing.



At n=8 all three methods achieved an approximation ratio of 1.000, meaning every method found the same maximum cut of 38.43. This confirms the implementations are correct and agree on small graphs.
Graph Structure (n=8)

Brute Force — Cut: 38.43 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 38.43 (ratio: 1.000)

QAOA — Cut: 37.65 (ratio: 0.980)





At n=10 the methods begin to diverge noticeably. Greedy drops to a ratio of 0.839 while QAOA holds at 0.959. This is the first graph size where the choice of algorithm starts to meaningfully affect solution quality.
Graph Structure (n=10)

Brute Force — Cut: 45.77 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 38.40 (ratio: 0.839)

QAOA — Cut: 43.90 (ratio: 0.959)





At n=30 brute force took 118 minutes to find the optimal cut while QAOA simulation took approximately 103 minutes. Both methods are expensive at this scale when run classically. The graph is noticeably more complex and the partition boundaries are harder to visually interpret, which reflects the increased difficulty of the problem.
Graph Structure (n=30)

Brute Force — Cut: 361.54 (ratio: 1.000)

Greedy — Cut: 303.28 (ratio: 0.839)

QAOA — Cut: 310.21 (ratio: 0.858)


More analysis and final results coming in the project evaluation post.
